title: Symphony No. 4 in G major
hook: Sleigh bells, a fiddling Death and a child’s song of heaven, in Mahler’s gentlest symphony.

painting.title: Self-Portrait with Death Playing the Fiddle
painting.pairingNote: Death leans over the painter’s shoulder and plays a one-string fiddle; Alma Mahler said this picture inspired the symphony’s second movement, where a retuned violin plays Death’s dance.

facts: Mahler began the symphony in the summer of 1899 at Bad Aussee and finished it in August 1900 at Maiernigg, on the Wörthersee, during his summer breaks from running the Vienna Court Opera.

It grew backwards from a song. In 1892 Mahler had set “Das himmlische Leben” (“The Heavenly Life”), a poem from the folk anthology *Des Knaben Wunderhorn* in which a child describes heaven as a feast. He called the song the “tapering spire” of the symphony. Its tunes are glimpsed in the first three movements, and a soprano sings it whole in the finale.
It is shorter than the two symphonies before it and uses his smallest orchestra, with no trombones or tuba. Mahler gave the movements no titles and published no programme.

The premiere, in Munich on 25 November 1901 with Mahler conducting, puzzled and angered much of the audience, and critics in Berlin and Vienna were harsh. After the Second World War it became one of his most popular works.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a sleigh-bell stroll that turns turbulent (I), Death fiddling a dance (II), a long, serene set of variations that opens onto heaven (III), a child’s song of heavenly feasting (IV).

movements.heading: Bedächtig, nicht eilen
movements.summary: Sleigh bells and flutes jingle for three bars, and the violins slide into a graceful, old-fashioned tune that has often been compared to Schubert. The opening sounds innocent, but the [[development|development]] grows crowded, strange and loud, until a trumpet calls everyone to order. The tune then returns as if nothing had happened.

mainIdeas.name: The bells
mainIdeas.description: sleigh bells and flutes in a jingling, slightly hesitant rhythm. They return in the finale.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, violins
mainIdeas.description: a graceful, bowing melody in G major.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, cellos
mainIdeas.description: a broad, singing tune, marked “broadly sung”.

stops.hear: Sleigh bells and flutes jingle; the violins slip in with a graceful tune
stops.happening: The introduction and theme 1, in G major

stops.hear: The cellos sing a broad, warm melody
Perky woodwinds and a playful dance tune; the opening tune comes back
The sleigh bells again; a solo violin and woodwinds play fragments
The music grows crowded and strange, themes pile up in distant keys, getting louder
A shattering climax; then a trumpet blares a short military call
The violins resume the opening tune quietly, in mid-phrase
Everything slows down; the music lingers over its tunes

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden quickening and a bright, cheerful close

notice: Listen to the trumpet call after the climax. Mahler later used it to open his Fifth Symphony.
The recapitulation does not start at the beginning of the tune but in the middle of a phrase, as if the music had simply been interrupted and picked up again.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Szell recorded the symphony with the Cleveland Orchestra and the soprano Judith Raskin in Severance Hall, Cleveland, on 1 and 2 October 1965. On the Spotify album the symphony is tracks 1–4.

movements.heading: In gemächlicher Bewegung, ohne Hast
movements.summary: Mahler once called this [[scherzo|scherzo]] “Freund Hein spielt auf”: Friend Hein, a folk name for Death, strikes up a tune. The leader of the violins plays a solo on a violin tuned a whole tone higher, which gives a harsh, rasping sound, like a village fiddler’s. The tune is eerie rather than terrifying. Between its appearances come two gentle [[landler|Ländler]]-like trios.

mainIdeas.name: Death’s fiddle
mainIdeas.description: a crooked, scraping tune on a solo violin tuned up a tone, a technique called [[scordatura|scordatura]].

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: a short phrase that introduces the fiddle each time.

mainIdeas.name: The trios
mainIdeas.description: lazy, cheerful country dances in F major, warmer and softer.

stops.hear: A horn call, then a solo violin with a harsh, scraping tune
The music relaxes into a lazy, swaying dance in clarinets and strings
The horn call and the scraping fiddle return
A trumpet call, then a gentler, waltz-like dance, interrupted by dark rumbles in the bass
The fiddle comes back, now less ghostly

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Soft woodwind chords, and the movement fades out uncertainly

notice: Compare the solo violin in this movement with the orchestra’s violins. The retuned instrument sounds tighter and coarser, which is exactly the effect Mahler wanted.

movements.heading: Ruhevoll (Poco adagio)
movements.summary: The heart of the symphony, and its longest movement. The cellos sing a calm, rocking melody over plucked basses, and a sad, lamenting theme for the oboe answers. Mahler alternates the two in a series of [[variation|variation]]s. Late in the movement the variations speed up, faster and faster, then stop. At the very end, without warning, the whole orchestra blazes out in E major, the gates of heaven opening, and the music dies away.

mainIdeas.name: Theme A
mainIdeas.description: a peaceful, cradle-like melody in the cellos over slowly plucked basses.

mainIdeas.name: Theme B
mainIdeas.description: a lament for the oboe, in the minor, which rises to anguished climaxes.

mainIdeas.name: The bell-like bass
mainIdeas.description: a slow, tolling figure in the low strings that is almost always present.

stops.hear: Low strings pluck slowly; the cellos sing a calm, rocking melody
stops.happening: Theme A, in G major. The plucking is [[pizzicato|pizzicato]]

stops.hear: Slower: the oboe plays a sad, aching tune in the minor
The lament swells to a loud, anguished climax, then sinks back
Theme A returns, livelier and more graceful
The lament again, more intense, with a sudden harsh outburst
Theme A in a gentle, flowing variation
stops.happening: The final set of variations begins

stops.hear: The variations get faster and faster, almost frantic, then stop suddenly
stops.happening: The race, and a sudden return to calm

stops.hear: Without warning, a huge, radiant E major chord; horns and trumpets play the tune of the finale

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: The music fades into a long, hushed close
stops.happening: The door is left open for the finale

notice: The E major outburst near the end comes out of near silence and soon sinks back into it. It is brief, yet the whole movement seems to lead to it.
Mahler said the movement came to him from the image of a tombstone carved with the figure of the dead person, arms folded, in eternal sleep.

movements.heading: Sehr behaglich
movements.summary: A soprano sings “Das himmlische Leben”, the song from which the symphony grew: heaven described by a child, as a place of dancing, feasting and saints in the kitchen. Mahler asks her to sing “with childlike, cheerful expression”. Between the verses, the sleigh bells of the first movement rush in. The last verse moves to E major, soft and mysterious, and the symphony ends in a whisper.

mainIdeas.name: The song tune
mainIdeas.description: a simple, skipping melody, first heard on the clarinet.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: the sleigh bells of the first movement, now wild and hurried.

mainIdeas.name: The chorale
mainIdeas.description: a slow, hymn-like phrase at the end of each verse, “Saint Peter in heaven looks on”.

stops.hear: A clarinet plays a simple, carefree tune
stops.happening: The orchestral prelude, in G major

stops.hear: The soprano sings “Wir genießen die himmlischen Freuden” (“We revel in heavenly pleasures”)
stops.happening: Verse 1: dancing and singing in heaven

stops.hear: The voice slows to a solemn, hymn-like phrase
stops.happening: A [[chorale|chorale]] for Saint Peter, who looks on

stops.hear: Sleigh bells and flutes burst in, fast and wild
stops.happening: The first movement’s bells as a refrain

stops.hear: A darker verse in the minor, with an urgent accompaniment
stops.happening: Verse 2: Herod the butcher, a lamb led to slaughter, the heavenly feast

stops.hear: The skipping tune returns
stops.happening: Verse 3: fruit, vegetables and fish for the heavenly table

stops.hear: A long, gentle, pastoral interlude
stops.happening: The music prepares the last verse

stops.hear: Very soft, in E major, over harp and low strings
stops.happening: Verse 4: no music on earth compares with heaven’s

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: The voice falls silent; harp and double basses fade away

notice: The text is naïve, but the music is not: listen for the second verse, where the joyful heaven includes a lamb led to its death, and the music turns uneasy.
The final verse sings that “all things awake to joy”. The music then grows quieter and quieter instead of louder.

threads.title: A song at the end
threads.body: The finale’s song existed eight years before the symphony. The sleigh bells, the trumpet’s tune in the E major blaze of the slow movement, and many melodic shapes all anticipate it, so the symphony seems to find its way to a song it already knew.

threads.title: Innocence with shadows
threads.body: Sleigh bells and a child’s heaven, but also Death’s fiddle, the oboe’s lament and a lamb led to the slaughter. Mahler keeps both in view.

threads.title: Ending soft and in another key
threads.body: The symphony starts in G major and ends in E major, very quietly. Instead of a triumph, it closes with a child’s vision fading away.
